courseTitle: Social Media Management VA: From Zero to First Client
courseDescription: A complete beginner-to-job-ready training program for aspiring Social Media Management Virtual Assistants. Covers the tools, daily skills, portfolio-building, resume and proposal writing, and how to land and manage your first social media client.
priceNote: One-time payment unlocks lifetime access to all modules, video lessons, quizzes, and your Certificate of Completion.

modules.title: Module 1: Starting Out as a Social Media VA

lessons.title: What Is a Social Media Management VA?

slides.heading: What Is a Social Media Management VA?
bullets: Welcome to your Social Media VA journey
Manages a brand's social presence remotely
Works with businesses of every size
slides.narration: Welcome to Module 1 of your Social Media Management VA training. A Social Media Management VA is a remote professional who plans, creates, schedules, and monitors content on a business's social media accounts - typically Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok - so the business owner doesn't have to do it themselves.

slides.heading: What a Social Media VA Actually Does Day to Day
bullets: Plans and schedules posts
Responds to comments and messages
Tracks what's working with analytics
slides.narration: On a typical day, a Social Media VA builds out a content calendar, designs or sources graphics, writes captions, schedules everything with a tool like Meta Business Suite or Later, replies to comments and DMs, and checks analytics to see which posts are performing well.

slides.heading: Why Businesses Hire a Social Media VA
bullets: Consistent posting without the owner's time
Access to someone who knows the platforms
Frees the owner to run their business
slides.narration: Most small business owners know they should be posting regularly, but don't have the time or the platform know-how to do it well. Hiring a Social Media VA means their pages stay active and professional, while they focus on serving their own customers.

slides.heading: Is This Niche Right for You?
bullets: You enjoy being creative and organized
You're comfortable learning new apps
You like seeing engagement and results
slides.narration: This niche is a great fit if you enjoy writing, design, and staying organized with a content calendar, and if you find it satisfying to watch a page's likes, comments, and followers grow because of work you did.

lessons.title: Skills and Traits of a Great Social Media VA

slides.heading: Core Skills You'll Build
bullets: Content planning and calendars
Basic graphic design
Writing engaging captions
slides.narration: Over this training, you'll build four core skills: planning content ahead of time with a calendar, designing simple graphics in Canva, writing captions that get people to stop scrolling, and reading analytics to know what to do more of.

slides.heading: Traits Clients Look For
bullets: Reliability - posts go out on schedule
Brand awareness - matching each client's voice
Good judgment - knowing what NOT to post
slides.narration: Clients trust Social Media VAs who are reliable about hitting the posting schedule, who take the time to match the brand's voice and style, and who use good judgment - for example, knowing to pause a scheduled post during a sensitive news event.

slides.heading: A Day in the Life
bullets: Morning: check comments and messages
Midday: draft or schedule new content
End of day: quick performance check
slides.narration: A typical day might start by clearing overnight comments and messages, move into drafting or scheduling the next batch of posts, and end with a quick look at how yesterday's posts performed - all of which can usually be done in a focused hour or two per client.

slides.heading: Where Growth Leads
bullets: Handle more platforms over time
Take on content strategy, not just posting
Manage several client accounts at once
slides.narration: As you gain experience, you can grow from just scheduling posts into helping plan a client's whole content strategy, and eventually manage several clients' accounts at the same time for a full-time income.

lessons.title: Understanding Client Goals and Brand Voice

slides.heading: Why Brand Voice Matters
bullets: Every business sounds different on purpose
Consistency builds trust with followers
Your job is to sound like THEM, not you
slides.narration: Brand voice is how a business 'talks' to its audience - playful, professional, warm, or bold. Your job as their Social Media VA is to write and post in that voice consistently, not to inject your own personal style.

slides.heading: Questions to Ask a New Client
bullets: Who is your ideal customer?
What tone do you want - fun, formal, warm?
What results matter most - sales, awareness, bookings?
slides.narration: Before writing a single post, ask your client who their ideal customer is, what tone they want their brand to have, and what result actually matters to them - more sales, more brand awareness, or more bookings, for example.

slides.heading: Building a Simple Brand Voice Guide
bullets: Write down 3-5 words that describe the tone
List words/phrases they use (and avoid)
Keep examples of posts they loved
slides.narration: A simple brand voice guide can be just half a page: three to five words describing the tone, a few phrases the brand likes to use or avoid, and one or two example posts the client already loved. Keep this on hand for every piece of content you create.

slides.heading: Staying Aligned Over Time
bullets: Check in regularly, don't assume
Ask for feedback on the first few posts
Update the guide as the brand evolves
slides.narration: Brand voice can shift over time, so check in with your client regularly, especially in the first few weeks, and don't be afraid to ask directly whether a post landed the way they wanted.

lessons.title: Setting Up Your Home Workspace for Social Media Work

slides.heading: What You Actually Need to Get Started
bullets: A laptop or desktop with a stable browser
Decent internet for uploading images/video
A quiet space for the occasional client call
slides.narration: You don't need expensive equipment to start - a reliable laptop, decent internet for uploading images and short videos, and a reasonably quiet space for client calls is enough to get going.

slides.heading: Organizing Client Files
bullets: One folder per client
Subfolders for photos, videos, and captions
A shared drive so clients can drop in assets
slides.narration: Keep every client's assets organized in their own folder, with subfolders for photos, videos, and caption drafts. A shared Google Drive or Dropbox folder also makes it easy for clients to drop in new photos whenever they have them.

slides.heading: Building a Simple Content Calendar Template
bullets: Date, platform, caption, and image columns
A status column - draft, approved, scheduled, posted
One tab per client keeps things simple
slides.narration: A basic spreadsheet with columns for date, platform, caption, image, and status - draft, approved, scheduled, or posted - is often all you need to stay organized, and it's something you'll build for real in Module 4.

slides.heading: Ready for Module 2
bullets: You know what the role involves
You understand brand voice
Next: the tools you'll actually use daily
slides.narration: You now understand what a Social Media Management VA does and why brand voice matters. In Module 2, we'll get hands-on with the actual tools you'll use every day on the job.

modules.title: Module 2: Essential Tools Every Social Media VA Must Know

slides.heading: Why Scheduling Tools Matter
bullets: Plan a whole week or month in advance
Post at the best times automatically
Manage multiple clients from one dashboard
slides.narration: Scheduling tools let you plan and queue up content ahead of time instead of manually posting every single day, and they let you manage several clients' accounts from a single dashboard.

slides.heading: Meta Business Suite
bullets: Free tool for Facebook and Instagram
Schedule posts, check inbox, see insights
Great starting tool - most clients already have it
slides.narration: Meta Business Suite is Meta's own free tool for managing Facebook and Instagram together - you can schedule posts, check messages and comments from both platforms in one inbox, and view basic performance insights.

slides.heading: Later and Buffer
bullets: Popular third-party scheduling tools
Visual calendar view of upcoming posts
Support more platforms, including TikTok
slides.narration: Later and Buffer are popular paid scheduling tools that show your content on a visual calendar and support more platforms than Meta Business Suite alone, including TikTok - useful once you're managing several clients.

slides.heading: Choosing the Right Tool per Client
bullets: Small client on a budget: Meta Business Suite
Client on multiple platforms: Later or Buffer
Always confirm who's paying for the tool
slides.narration: For a client who's only active on Facebook and Instagram, Meta Business Suite is usually enough and free. For a client active on more platforms, a paid tool like Later may be worth it - just confirm upfront whether you or the client covers that cost.

slides.heading: Why Canva Is a Social Media VA's Best Friend
bullets: Free, browser-based design tool
Thousands of ready-made social media templates
No design degree required
slides.narration: Canva is a free, browser-based design tool with thousands of ready-made templates sized specifically for Instagram posts, Stories, Facebook covers, and more - you don't need any design background to create professional-looking graphics.

slides.heading: Working With Brand Kits
bullets: Save a client's logo, fonts, and colors once
Apply them to any template in one click
Keeps every post looking consistently on-brand
slides.narration: Canva's Brand Kit feature lets you save a client's logo, brand colors, and fonts once, then apply them to any template with a click - this is how you keep every single post looking consistently on-brand without redoing work each time.

slides.heading: Resizing for Every Platform
bullets: One design, multiple platform sizes
Canva's Magic Resize handles most of it
Always double-check text doesn't get cut off
slides.narration: Canva can automatically resize one design into the different dimensions each platform needs - a square Instagram post, a vertical Story, a Facebook cover photo - though it's good practice to double-check that text and logos aren't cropped after resizing.

slides.heading: Building a Simple Template Library
bullets: Save your best-performing designs as templates
Duplicate and swap text/photos for new posts
Saves hours once you have a library built
slides.narration: As you work with a client, save your best-performing post designs as reusable templates. For future posts, you just duplicate and swap the text and photo - this can turn a 20-minute design task into a 3-minute one.

slides.heading: Connecting Facebook and Instagram Accounts
bullets: Link both accounts under one Meta Business Suite
Client stays the account owner, you get access as admin
Never ask for a client's personal password
slides.narration: You'll typically be added as an admin or editor on a client's Facebook Page and connected Instagram account through Meta Business Suite - the client always stays the actual owner, and you should never need their personal login password.

slides.heading: Understanding Facebook Pages vs Personal Profiles
bullets: Businesses should use a Page, not a personal profile
Pages allow multiple admins and ads
Personal profiles can't be safely shared with a VA
slides.narration: A Facebook Page (not a personal profile) is what businesses should be using - it supports multiple admins, allows running ads, and is the only safe way to give a VA access without sharing a personal account.

slides.heading: Instagram Basics for VAs
bullets: Feed posts, Stories, and Reels are different formats
Reels currently get the most reach for most brands
Hashtags and captions still matter for discovery
slides.narration: Instagram gives you three main formats to work with: feed posts, 24-hour Stories, and short-form Reels - Reels currently tend to get the most reach for most business accounts, so many clients will want a steady mix that includes them.

slides.heading: Reading the Meta Business Suite Inbox
bullets: Comments and DMs from both platforms in one place
Respond promptly - speed matters for engagement
Flag anything sensitive for the client to handle
slides.narration: The Meta Business Suite inbox brings Facebook and Instagram comments and messages into one place, which makes it much easier to respond quickly - and speed matters, since fast replies boost a post's visibility. Always flag sensitive complaints for your client rather than responding on your own.

slides.heading: Why TikTok Is Different
bullets: Short-form video, not photos or long captions
Discovery-driven - strangers see your content constantly
Trends and sounds matter a lot
slides.narration: TikTok is built entirely around short-form video and works very differently from Facebook or Instagram - its algorithm shows your content to strangers constantly based on interest, not just to existing followers, and using trending sounds or formats really does help.

slides.heading: Setting Up a TikTok Business Account
bullets: Switch to a Business account for analytics
Add a link and contact info to the bio
Business accounts unlock the commercial sound library
slides.narration: A TikTok Business account (free to switch to) unlocks analytics, lets you add a website link and contact button to the bio, and gives access to a commercial sound library that's safe to use for business content.

slides.heading: Simple Content Ideas That Work
bullets: Behind-the-scenes clips of the business
Quick tips related to the client's industry
Trending sounds paired with the client's product
slides.narration: You don't need a professional camera crew - behind-the-scenes clips, quick tips related to the client's industry, and trending sounds paired with everyday footage of the client's product or service are simple, effective starting points.

slides.heading: Repurposing Content Across Platforms
bullets: One video can become a TikTok, Reel, and Story
Saves time versus creating separate content per platform
Always adjust captions to fit each platform's tone
slides.narration: A single short video can usually be posted as a TikTok, an Instagram Reel, and a Facebook Story with only minor changes - this repurposing is one of the biggest time-savers for a Social Media VA managing multiple platforms.

slides.heading: Why Analytics Matter to Your Clients
bullets: Proves the value of your work
Shows what content to make more of
Justifies your rate at renewal time
slides.narration: Analytics aren't just numbers - they prove to your client that your work is paying off, show you exactly what type of content to make more of, and give you real evidence to justify your rate when a contract renews.

slides.heading: Key Metrics to Track
bullets: Reach - how many people saw the post
Engagement - likes, comments, shares, saves
Follower growth over time
slides.narration: The three metrics worth tracking for almost any client are reach, which is how many people saw a post; engagement, meaning likes, comments, shares, and saves; and overall follower growth over time.

slides.heading: Where to Find the Numbers
bullets: Meta Business Suite Insights tab
Instagram's built-in Insights (for Business accounts)
TikTok Analytics under Business account settings
slides.narration: Meta Business Suite has a built-in Insights tab covering Facebook and Instagram together, Instagram's own app has Insights for Business accounts, and TikTok Analytics is available once you've switched to a Business account.

slides.heading: Building a Simple Monthly Report
bullets: One page: top 3 posts, key numbers, next month's plan
Use screenshots - clients rarely want raw spreadsheets
Send it on the same date every month
slides.narration: A simple one-page monthly report - your top 3 performing posts, the key numbers, and a short plan for next month - is usually all a client wants. Screenshots of the actual analytics dashboards are often more convincing than a spreadsheet, and sending it on the same date each month builds trust.

modules.title: Module 3: Core Social Media Management Skills

slides.heading: What a Content Calendar Actually Is
bullets: A plan of what posts when, on which platform
Usually built one to four weeks ahead
Prevents last-minute scrambling for ideas
slides.narration: A content calendar is simply a plan of what gets posted, when, and on which platform - usually mapped out one to four weeks in advance, so you're never scrambling for an idea the morning a post is due.

slides.heading: A Simple Weekly Structure
bullets: Mix of content types - not just promotions
Educational, behind-the-scenes, promotional, engagement
A rough ratio like 40/30/20/10 works well
slides.narration: A healthy weekly mix might be about 40% educational or helpful content, 30% behind-the-scenes, 20% direct promotion, and 10% pure engagement posts like questions or polls - constant selling alone tends to lose followers over time.

slides.heading: Sourcing Content Ideas
bullets: Client's FAQs make great educational posts
Repurpose blog posts, testimonials, and reviews
Keep a running idea list, don't start from zero
slides.narration: Some of the best content ideas come straight from a client's frequently asked questions, existing blog posts, or customer testimonials and reviews - keep a running list of ideas so you're never starting from a blank page.

slides.heading: Getting Client Approval Efficiently
bullets: Share the calendar a week or two ahead
One clear approval step, not endless back-and-forth
Batch small edits instead of one-by-one
slides.narration: Share the upcoming calendar with your client a week or two in advance, and set a clear single approval step rather than an endless back-and-forth - batching any small edit requests together saves everyone time.

slides.heading: The Anatomy of a Strong Caption
bullets: A hook in the first line
The message or value in the middle
A clear call-to-action at the end
slides.narration: A strong caption usually has three parts: a hook in the very first line that stops the scroll, the actual message or value in the middle, and a clear call-to-action at the end telling the reader exactly what to do next.

slides.heading: Writing Hooks That Stop the Scroll
bullets: Ask a relatable question
Make a bold or surprising statement
Call out the exact audience you want
slides.narration: Strong hooks often ask a relatable question, make a bold or surprising statement, or call out the exact audience the post is for - for example, starting with 'If you're a busy mom juggling errands...' immediately tells the right people this post is for them.

slides.heading: Matching Caption Length to the Platform
bullets: Instagram/Facebook: short-to-medium works well
TikTok: keep it very short, video does the talking
Longer isn't always better - clarity wins
slides.narration: Instagram and Facebook captions can be short to medium length depending on the topic, but TikTok captions should stay very short since the video itself is doing most of the talking - in every case, clarity beats length.

slides.heading: Calls-to-Action That Actually Work
bullets: Comment your answer below
Send us a message to book
Tag a friend who needs this
slides.narration: Effective calls-to-action are specific and easy to do right there in the app - 'Comment your answer below,' 'Send us a message to book your spot,' or 'Tag a friend who needs to see this' all give a clear, simple next step.

slides.heading: Why Fast Responses Matter
bullets: Platforms reward posts with quick engagement
Customers expect a same-day reply
Silence can look like the business doesn't care
slides.narration: Platforms tend to show a post to more people when it gets quick engagement, and customers today generally expect a reply within the same day - leaving comments and messages unanswered can make a business look like it doesn't care.

slides.heading: Responding to Positive Comments
bullets: Reply with genuine warmth, not a generic 'thanks!'
Use the commenter's name when possible
Encourage further engagement when it fits
slides.narration: Positive comments deserve more than a generic 'thanks!' - replying with genuine warmth, using the person's name when you can, and occasionally asking a friendly follow-up question keeps the conversation going and builds real community.

slides.heading: Handling Negative Comments Professionally
bullets: Stay calm and professional, never defensive
Move detailed complaints to DM or email
Always loop in your client for anything serious
slides.narration: Negative comments should be handled calmly and professionally - acknowledge the concern publicly, then move detailed back-and-forth to a private message or email, and always loop your client in on anything that looks serious, like a threat of a bad review.

slides.heading: Setting Response Time Expectations With Clients
bullets: Agree on a response-time target upfront
Clarify which messages you can answer vs escalate
Document common Q&A answers for consistency
slides.narration: Agree with your client upfront on a realistic response-time target, and clarify which types of questions you're expected to answer directly versus escalate to them - a simple shared document of common questions and approved answers keeps your replies consistent.

slides.heading: What Hashtags Actually Do
bullets: Help new people discover a post
Group content by topic or community
Work differently on each platform
slides.narration: Hashtags help a post get discovered by people who don't already follow the account, by grouping it with other content on the same topic - though how much they matter, and how many to use, varies by platform.

slides.heading: Choosing the Right Hashtags
bullets: Mix broad, niche, and local hashtags
Research what similar accounts actually use
Avoid banned or overused generic tags
slides.narration: A good hashtag set usually mixes a few broad, high-volume tags with more specific niche tags and, for local businesses, location-based tags - it helps to research what similar, successful accounts are actually using rather than guessing.

slides.heading: Organic Growth Tactics Beyond Hashtags
bullets: Collaborate or get tagged by other accounts
Engage genuinely on other relevant accounts
Post consistently - algorithms reward consistency
slides.narration: Beyond hashtags, real growth comes from collaborating with or getting tagged by other accounts, genuinely engaging on other relevant pages (not just your own), and simply posting consistently, since most platforms reward accounts that show up reliably.

slides.heading: Setting Realistic Growth Expectations With Clients
bullets: Growth is usually gradual, not overnight
Set monthly, not daily, growth goals
Educate clients so they don't expect instant virality
slides.narration: It's part of your job to set realistic expectations - most accounts grow gradually over months, not overnight, so agreeing on monthly rather than daily goals, and gently educating clients that going viral isn't guaranteed, protects the relationship.

modules.title: Module 4: Building Your Social Media Portfolio

lessons.title: Creating Sample Content Calendars and Mock Campaigns

slides.heading: Why You Need Samples Before Your First Client
bullets: Clients want to see proof, not just a resume
A mock project shows your actual thinking
You control the quality - no client pressure yet
slides.narration: Since you may not have a paying client yet, building a mock content calendar and campaign for a fictional or real local business lets you show proof of your skills, not just claim them on a resume - and you control the quality with no deadline pressure.

slides.heading: Picking a Practice Business
bullets: Choose an industry you understand well
A real local shop works great (with permission)
Or invent a believable fictional brand
slides.narration: Pick an industry you already understand - maybe a coffee shop, a boutique, or a local gym. You can build a sample around a real business you admire (with their knowledge) or a believable fictional brand you invent yourself.

slides.heading: Building a One-Month Mock Calendar
bullets: Plan roughly 12-16 posts across a month
Mix content types using the 40/30/20/10 idea
Write full captions, not just topic ideas
slides.narration: Build out a full month - about 12 to 16 posts - using the content-type mix you learned in Module 3, and write COMPLETE captions for each post rather than just rough topic ideas, since finished work is what impresses a future client.

slides.heading: Designing the Actual Graphics
bullets: Use Canva to design each post visually
Keep a consistent look across the whole set
Export everything neatly into one shared folder
slides.narration: Design the actual graphics in Canva for at least several of your mock posts, keeping a consistent visual style throughout, then export and organize everything into one clean, shareable folder.

lessons.title: Building a Social Media Management Portfolio

slides.heading: What a Social Media Portfolio Needs
bullets: A short intro about you and your specialty
2-3 sample projects with visuals
Your process, not just the pretty pictures
slides.narration: A strong portfolio has a short introduction about who you are and what you specialize in, two or three sample projects with real visuals, and a brief explanation of your process - clients want to understand HOW you think, not just see finished graphics.

slides.heading: Where to Host Your Portfolio
bullets: A simple free website (Canva, Carrd, or similar)
A well-organized Google Drive folder works too
Keep the link short and easy to share
slides.narration: You don't need a paid website - a simple site built for free in Canva or Carrd, or even a neatly organized, view-only Google Drive folder, works perfectly well as long as the link is short and easy to share in a proposal or DM.

slides.heading: Presenting Before/After or Results
bullets: Show growth numbers if you have any (even mock)
Use simple before/after screenshots
Be honest - don't fabricate real client results
slides.narration: If you have any real results, even small ones, show them with simple before-and-after screenshots or numbers. For mock projects, be upfront that they're sample work rather than real client results - honesty builds more trust than an impressive but fake number.

slides.heading: Keeping Your Portfolio Updated
bullets: Swap in real client work as soon as you have it
Remove your weakest samples over time
Revisit it every few months
slides.narration: As soon as you land real client work (with their permission to showcase it), swap it in for your mock samples, and keep quietly removing your weakest pieces over time so your portfolio only ever shows your current best work.

slides.heading: Why Results Convert Better Than Promises
bullets: Numbers build trust faster than claims
Clients hire outcomes, not just tasks
Even small wins are worth showing
slides.narration: A specific number - even a modest one, like '30% more comments in 6 weeks' - builds trust faster than a vague promise, because it shows you deliver outcomes, not just busywork.

slides.heading: What to Track From Day One With a New Client
bullets: Screenshot starting follower count and engagement
Note the date you started managing the account
Repeat the same screenshot monthly
slides.narration: From the very first day with a new client, screenshot their starting follower count and recent engagement numbers, note the exact date you began, and repeat that same screenshot every month - this makes an honest before/after comparison easy to produce later.

slides.heading: Turning Numbers Into a Simple Case Study
bullets: One paragraph: the challenge
One paragraph: what you did
One paragraph: the result, with a number
slides.narration: A simple case study is just three short paragraphs: what challenge the client had, what you actually did about it, and what result followed - ideally with a real number attached to that last part.

slides.heading: Getting Permission to Share Results Publicly
bullets: Always ask before using a client's name or numbers
Some clients prefer to stay anonymous - that's fine
A quick written 'yes' protects you both
slides.narration: Always ask a client's permission before sharing their name, page, or specific numbers publicly - some are happy to be named, others prefer anonymity, and either way a quick written yes over email or chat protects you both.

modules.title: Module 5: Resume and Job Application Mastery for Social Media VAs

lessons.title: Writing a Social Media VA Resume

slides.heading: What Belongs on a Social Media VA Resume
bullets: A clear headline naming your specialty
Tools you know - Canva, Meta Business Suite, etc.
A link to your portfolio, front and center
slides.narration: Your resume should open with a clear headline naming your specialty - 'Social Media Management VA' - list the specific tools you know like Canva and Meta Business Suite, and put your portfolio link somewhere it can't be missed.

slides.heading: Describing Experience Without a Job History
bullets: Frame your training and mock projects as real work
Use action verbs - planned, designed, scheduled
Quantify wherever you can, even mock numbers
slides.narration: If you don't have paid experience yet, describe your training and mock campaigns using strong action verbs - planned, designed, scheduled, analyzed - and quantify what you can, like 'planned a 16-post monthly content calendar.'

slides.heading: Formatting for Readability
bullets: Keep it to one page
Use short bullet points, not paragraphs
Consistent, clean font and spacing
slides.narration: Keep your resume to a single page with short, scannable bullet points rather than dense paragraphs, using a clean, consistent font - a client reviewing dozens of applicants will spend only seconds per resume.

slides.heading: Common Resume Mistakes to Avoid
bullets: Vague phrases like 'social media expert'
No portfolio link at all
Typos - always proofread out loud
slides.narration: Avoid vague self-descriptions like 'social media expert' with nothing to back it up, never submit a resume without your portfolio link, and always proofread out loud before sending - typos undercut your credibility instantly in this field.

lessons.title: Crafting Winning Proposals for Social Media Clients

slides.heading: What a Good Proposal Includes
bullets: A quick summary of their current social presence
Your specific plan for improving it
Clear pricing and next steps
slides.narration: A strong proposal briefly summarizes what you noticed about their current social media, lays out your specific plan for improving it, and ends with clear pricing and an easy next step, like a short call.

slides.heading: Personalizing Every Proposal
bullets: Reference their actual page and recent posts
Never send an obviously copy-pasted pitch
Mention one specific opportunity you spotted
slides.narration: Every proposal should reference the client's actual page and something specific you noticed - an inconsistent posting schedule, an untapped platform, or an opportunity you spotted - a generic copy-pasted pitch is easy to spot and easy to ignore.

slides.heading: Structuring Your Pricing
bullets: Package by deliverables - posts, stories, engagement
Offer 2-3 clear tiers, not endless options
Be upfront about what's NOT included
slides.narration: Package your pricing around clear deliverables - for example, a certain number of posts and stories per week, plus daily engagement - and offer two or three simple tiers rather than overwhelming a client with options. Be upfront about what falls outside the package too.

slides.heading: Following Up Without Being Pushy
bullets: One polite follow-up after about a week
Add new value, don't just 'check in'
Know when to move on gracefully
slides.narration: If you don't hear back, one polite follow-up after about a week is reasonable - ideally adding something new, like a quick content idea for their page, rather than just 'checking in.' If there's still no response after that, it's fine to move on gracefully.

lessons.title: Where to Find Social Media VA Clients

slides.heading: Freelance Platforms
bullets: Upwork, Onlinejobs.ph, and similar sites
Filter for social media / content roles
A strong profile and portfolio link matter most
slides.narration: Freelance platforms like Upwork and Onlinejobs.ph list social media and content roles regularly - filter specifically for those, and make sure your profile headline and portfolio link are strong, since clients often decide in seconds.

slides.heading: Local Small Businesses
bullets: Coffee shops, salons, gyms, boutiques nearby
Many have inactive or outdated pages
A polite, specific outreach message works well
slides.narration: Local small businesses - coffee shops, salons, gyms, boutiques - are often sitting on inactive or outdated social pages simply because the owner is busy running the business. A polite, specific outreach message pointing out one thing you could improve for them works well.

slides.heading: Referrals and Word of Mouth
bullets: Your first client is your best source of the next
Ask happy clients if they know anyone else
A short testimonial makes referrals even easier
slides.narration: Once you land one happy client, ask directly whether they know any other business owners who could use similar help - referrals convert far more easily than cold outreach, especially if you have a short testimonial to share.

slides.heading: Facebook Groups and Communities
bullets: Local business groups often post 'looking for help'
VA and freelancer communities share leads too
Be an active, helpful member, not just a lurker
slides.narration: Local business Facebook groups often have owners posting that they need social media help, and dedicated VA or freelancer communities frequently share leads too - being an active, genuinely helpful member of these groups (not just posting your own ads) tends to bring in the best opportunities.

slides.heading: What Clients Are Actually Evaluating
bullets: Can you understand their brand quickly?
Do you ask smart, specific questions?
Will you be easy and pleasant to work with?
slides.narration: In a discovery call, clients aren't just checking your skills on paper - they're watching whether you can understand their brand quickly, whether you ask smart and specific questions, and whether you seem easy and pleasant to work with.

slides.heading: Questions You Should Ask Them
bullets: What does success look like to you?
What's frustrated you about social media so far?
Who else is involved in approving content?
slides.narration: Come prepared with your own questions: what does success actually look like to them, what's frustrated them about social media so far, and who else needs to approve content - this shows you're thinking like a real partner, not just an order-taker.

slides.heading: Talking About Pricing Confidently
bullets: Know your rate before the call, don't improvise
Explain what's included, not just the number
It's okay to say you'll follow up in writing
slides.narration: Decide your rate before the call so you're never improvising under pressure, explain clearly what's included for that price, and it's completely fine to say you'll send the full proposal in writing afterward rather than negotiating on the spot.

slides.heading: Following Up After the Call
bullets: Send a written summary within 24 hours
Restate what you understood about their needs
Attach your proposal or next steps clearly
slides.narration: Within 24 hours of the call, send a short written summary restating what you understood about their needs, attached to your proposal or a clear next step - this reinforces that you listened closely and keeps momentum going.

modules.title: Module 6: Landing Your First Social Media Client and Beyond

lessons.title: Onboarding a New Social Media Client

slides.heading: What Onboarding Actually Covers
bullets: Getting access to their accounts safely
Gathering brand assets and guidelines
Agreeing on the first month's plan
slides.narration: Onboarding is the process of getting properly set up with a new client: gaining safe access to their accounts, collecting their logo and brand assets, and agreeing together on what the first month will actually look like.

slides.heading: Getting Account Access the Right Way
bullets: Ask to be added as admin/editor on Business Suite
Never ask for personal account passwords
Confirm who owns the account long-term
slides.narration: Always ask to be added as an admin or editor through Meta Business Suite rather than requesting a personal password - this is safer for both of you, and it makes clear that the client remains the true, permanent owner of the account.

slides.heading: Collecting Brand Assets
bullets: Logo files, brand colors, and fonts
Existing photos or product images
Any brand guidelines document, if one exists
slides.narration: Request the client's logo files, brand colors and fonts, any existing product or team photos, and a brand guidelines document if they have one - having these upfront saves a lot of back-and-forth later.

slides.heading: Setting the First 30 Days' Plan
bullets: Agree on posting frequency and platforms
Set your first check-in date
Clarify how and when you'll be paid
slides.narration: Before posting anything, agree on how often you'll post and on which platforms, set a date for your first check-in call, and make sure payment terms - amount, method, and schedule - are clearly agreed on both sides.

lessons.title: Setting Expectations and Pricing Your Services

slides.heading: Why Clear Expectations Prevent Problems
bullets: Most client conflicts come from unspoken assumptions
A short written agreement protects you both
Revisit and adjust as the relationship grows
slides.narration: Most conflicts between a VA and a client come from things that were never actually agreed on out loud - a short written agreement covering scope, pricing, and response times protects you both and can always be revisited as things grow.

slides.heading: Common Pricing Models
bullets: Monthly retainer - most common for ongoing work
Per-project - for one-off campaigns
Hourly - less common, harder to scale
slides.narration: A monthly retainer is the most common model for ongoing social media management, a per-project rate suits one-off campaigns like a product launch, and hourly pricing is less common in this niche since it's harder to scale as you take on more clients.

slides.heading: What to Include in Your Scope of Work
bullets: Number of posts/platforms included
What counts as a 'revision' vs a new request
What's explicitly NOT included (e.g. paid ads)
slides.narration: Your scope of work should spell out exactly how many posts and which platforms are included, what counts as a normal revision versus a brand-new request, and what's explicitly NOT included, like running paid ad campaigns, unless you charge separately for that.

slides.heading: Raising Your Rates Over Time
bullets: Review rates as your skill and results grow
Give existing clients advance notice
New clients can start at your current rate
slides.narration: As your skills and track record grow, it's normal and healthy to raise your rates - give existing clients advance notice (30-60 days is common), while any brand-new client simply starts at your current, updated rate.

slides.heading: Staying Organized Across Clients
bullets: One shared calendar tool, separate client views
Color-code or label content by client
A weekly planning block prevents last-minute chaos
slides.narration: Managing several clients well usually comes down to using one scheduling tool for everyone (most support multiple client accounts), color-coding or labeling content clearly by client, and setting aside a dedicated weekly block to plan ahead rather than reacting day to day.

slides.heading: Avoiding Mix-Ups Between Clients
bullets: Double-check the account before every post
Never reuse a caption meant for another client
Build a simple pre-post checklist
slides.narration: Posting to the wrong account is a real and embarrassing risk once you're juggling multiple clients - always double-check which account you're in before posting, never copy-paste a caption written for one client into another's queue, and consider a short pre-post checklist.

slides.heading: Batching Work for Efficiency
bullets: Design a week's graphics in one sitting
Write a batch of captions together
Batch client communications too
slides.narration: Batching similar tasks - designing a whole week of graphics in one sitting, writing several captions back to back, or replying to all client messages at set times - is far more efficient than constantly switching between different types of work.

slides.heading: Knowing When You've Reached Capacity
bullets: Quality should never quietly slip as you add clients
Track your actual hours per client honestly
It's okay to pause new clients or raise rates instead
slides.narration: Watch for signs that quality is slipping as you take on more clients - missed deadlines, rushed captions, slower replies. Track your real hours per client honestly, and remember it's completely fine to pause taking new clients, or raise your rates instead of stretching yourself too thin.

slides.heading: Receiving Feedback Without Getting Defensive
bullets: Feedback is about the work, not you personally
Ask clarifying questions before revising
Thank the client for being specific
slides.narration: It's easy to feel personally criticized when a client pushes back on a caption or design, but feedback is about the work, not you - ask clarifying questions if something's vague, and genuinely thank clients who give specific, actionable feedback.

slides.heading: Handling Vague Feedback
bullets: 'I don't love it' needs more detail
Offer 2-3 specific directions to choose from
Show, don't just ask - options speed things up
slides.narration: When feedback is vague, like 'I don't love it, try again,' ask what specifically isn't working, and consider offering two or three specific alternative directions rather than an open-ended redo - showing options is often faster than endless back-and-forth.

slides.heading: Managing Scope Creep in Revisions
bullets: Define how many revision rounds are included
A brand-new concept isn't a 'revision'
Politely price extra requests separately
slides.narration: Define upfront how many rounds of revision are included per post - a request for a completely new concept, rather than a tweak to the current one, isn't really a 'revision,' and it's fair to politely price that as an additional request.

slides.heading: Turning Difficult Clients Into Long-Term Ones
bullets: Most 'difficult' clients just want to feel heard
Consistent, calm communication builds trust
Know when a client truly isn't the right fit
slides.narration: Many clients who seem difficult at first just want to feel heard and kept in the loop - consistent, calm communication usually turns them into your most loyal clients over time. Occasionally, though, a client genuinely isn't the right fit, and it's okay to part ways professionally.

lessons.title: Growing Your Social Media VA Career

slides.heading: Leveling Up Your Skill Set
bullets: Learn basic paid ads (Meta Ads Manager)
Get comfortable with simple video editing
Study analytics more deeply over time
slides.narration: As you grow, learning basic paid advertising through Meta Ads Manager, getting comfortable with simple video editing (even in free apps like CapCut), and studying analytics more deeply all let you charge more and take on bigger clients.

slides.heading: Deciding Between More Clients or Higher Rates
bullets: More clients means more income but more hours
Higher rates mean the same hours, more income
Most successful VAs eventually favor the second
slides.narration: At some point you'll choose between taking on more clients at your current rate, or fewer clients at a higher rate - most experienced Social Media VAs eventually favor raising rates over endlessly adding more clients, since it protects both quality and your own time.

slides.heading: Building Toward an Agency or Team
bullets: Some VAs eventually hire their own subcontractors
Others stay solo and simply raise rates
Both paths are valid - choose what fits your goals
slides.narration: Some experienced Social Media VAs eventually build a small team, subcontracting design or scheduling work to other freelancers and keeping strategy for themselves; others prefer staying solo and simply commanding premium rates. Neither path is more 'correct' - it depends on what kind of work-life you actually want.

slides.heading: Congratulations on Finishing This Training
bullets: You've covered the full Social Media VA skillset
You have a portfolio, resume, and pricing plan
Time to start applying with confidence
slides.narration: Congratulations - you've now covered the full Social Media Management VA skillset, from the tools and daily skills to portfolio-building, client acquisition, and long-term growth. You're ready to start applying and pitching with real confidence.
